Retirement withdrawals: why the order of returns changes the plan

Compare two portfolios with the same ten returns in reverse order, then isolate what changes when retirement spending is withdrawn.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

The central idea

Once a portfolio funds spending, the order of returns matters. A long-run average alone cannot describe the path of available retirement capital.

01

Compare two paths with the same ingredients

The first chart uses ten invented annual returns. One sequence begins with losses of 20% and 10%; the other reverses the entire sequence. Starting capital and the withdrawal rule are identical. Both sequences contain exactly the same returns.

Withdrawals occur at the start of each year, before that year’s return applies. This convention is deliberately explicit because moving the payment date changes the result. The selected annual increase raises requested spending each year; it does not change the return series.

Schwab’s sequence-risk explanation describes how early losses can be particularly damaging when a portfolio is funding withdrawals. Our chart uses its own invented return series and assumptions, rather than copying Schwab’s example or estimating a historical retirement outcome.

02

Read the return bars before interpreting the balance

The grouped bars show the annual return in each sequence. Negative values fall below zero. Their order differs, but their arithmetic average and no-withdrawal compounded return are the same.

With no deposits or withdrawals, the ending balance is the starting amount multiplied by all ten return factors. Reordering multiplication does not change that product. Intermediate balances still differ, which can matter for liquidity and behaviour even in the no-withdrawal case.

Set the withdrawal to zero and inspect the final balances. They should match up to rounding. That comparison acts as a control: it helps isolate the role of cash flows instead of attributing every difference to a change in average investment performance.

03

Why the withdrawal changes the arithmetic

When money is withdrawn, it no longer participates in subsequent gains or losses. A poor early return can leave a smaller balance supporting later withdrawals. The same dollar spending can then consume a greater fraction of the remaining portfolio.

The recurrence used here is ending balance = (opening balance − funded withdrawal) × (1 + annual return). Funded withdrawal cannot exceed available assets. If requested spending is larger, the remaining balance is zero and the unmet amount is recorded separately.

The tool reports unfunded withdrawals because a zero balance must not look like a successfully financed spending plan. In a depleted path, actual funded spending can differ between the two sequences even though the requested rule is identical.

04

Keep a teaching comparison separate from a retirement forecast

Ten hand-picked returns cannot establish a sustainable withdrawal rate or a probability of success. There is no statistical confidence interval here, no simulation distribution and no claim that either sequence is likely to occur.

A full plan also needs a longer horizon, longevity assumptions, pension and benefit cash flows, taxes, investment costs, asset allocation, inflation and spending flexibility. Currency and household obligations can add further constraints. Those items are outside this demonstration.

Do not treat the first withdrawal as a recommended percentage of savings. It is an input that exposes the relationship. A plan that works under one invented sequence may fail under a different drawdown, a longer life or a larger spending need.

05

Use the charts to ask better planning questions

  1. Which essential expenses are covered by reliable income outside the portfolio?
  2. How much spending could be delayed or reduced after a market decline?
  3. What liquid resources are available without selling volatile assets?
  4. How would a longer retirement or a higher cost level change the funding gap?
  5. When will the withdrawal plan be reviewed and adjusted?

Flexibility can change the required cash flows, while asset allocation changes the range of investment paths. Neither can be assessed from a single average return. Use this visual explanation as a starting point for a plan with explicit obligations, documented assumptions and a review process.
